Q: Query with LIKE / IN A:

Since the RDBMS is not specified in the question and tags, we can look at an example for Postgresql.

Using comma‑separated lists of values, as is already being actively discussed in this question (as well as in many other SO questions), is considered a wrong approach to database design.

In this case, the “article” table stores tickers in the form of a list.
It is proposed to create an additional table “article_ticker” (article_id, ticker_id) to normalize the database and use indexes for fast linking between these tables and apply filters.
Some DBMS extensions allow for more convenient and efficient work with such values. Of course, in a more formalized form — JSON or ARRAY. The structured nature of the list enables more efficient work with it.

I suggest considering an example using GIN (General inverted index).

GIN is designed for handling cases where the items to be indexed are composite values, and the queries to be handled by the index need to search for element values that appear within the composite items. For example, the items could be documents, and the queries could be searches for documents containing specific words.

Comma-delimited tickers list stored as array.

It can be said that GIN creates an indexed list of tickers and implicitly associates a B‑Tree index of ticker‑>articles with them.

Table for example

CREATE TABLE article (
  article_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY generated always as identity,
  title varchar(20),
  article_txt TEXT NOT NULL,
  tickers text array 
);

Sample data

INSERT INTO article (title,article_txt,tickers) VALUES 
 ('article1 title', 'article1 text', array['AAPL','IBM'])
,('article2 title', 'article2 text', array['F','IBM'])
,('article3 title', 'article3 text', array['DELL','TXN'])
,('article4 title', 'article4 text', array['ALP','META']);

Query and output

SELECT *
FROM article a
WHERE array['AAPL','IBM','DELL','UNP'] && tickers ;

 article_id |     title      |  article_txt  |  tickers   
------------+----------------+---------------+------------
          1 | article1 title | article1 text | {AAPL,IBM}
          2 | article2 title | article2 text | {F,IBM}
          3 | article3 title | article3 text | {DELL,TXN}

Since the difference in approaches affects large tables, we’ll add more rows.

with src as ( -- full list of tickers
  select array['AAPL','IBM','F','IBM','DELL','TXN','ALP','META','TKT1'] AS ta
)
insert into article (title,article_txt,tickers)
select concat('article1 title',idx) AS title
    ,concat('article1 text',idx) AS article_txt
    ,array_sample(ta,cast(floor(random()*5)+1 as int))  AS tickers  -- arbitrary subset
from generate_series(1,429000) idx
cross join src;

Here we add rows with a list of tickers — an arbitrary subset of the full list.

The query that OP wants to implement looks like this in this case.

SELECT *
FROM article a
WHERE array['AAPL','IBM','DELL','UNP'] && tickers ;

I.e., select rows for which the condition array['AAPL','IBM','DELL','UNP'] && tickers

  • at least one ticker from the row belongs to the list specified by the parameter.

In the query execution plan, we expect to see a “table scan.”

QUERY PLAN                                                                
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Gather  (cost=1000.00..9920.08 rows=6794 width=126) (actual time=0.216..91.190 rows=343451.00 loops=1)
   Output: article_id, title, article_txt, tickers
   Workers Planned: 2
   Workers Launched: 2
   Buffers: shared hit=6748
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on public.article a  (cost=0.00..8240.68 rows=2831 width=126) (actual time=0.137..67.214 rows=114483.67 loops=3)
         Output: article_id, title, article_txt, tickers
         Filter: ('{AAPL,IBM,DELL,UNP}'::text[] && a.tickers)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 28518
         Buffers: shared hit=6748
         Worker 0:  actual time=0.191..61.626 rows=112368.00 loops=1
           Buffers: shared hit=2252
         Worker 1:  actual time=0.211..79.675 rows=83396.00 loops=1
           Buffers: shared hit=1722
 Planning Time: 0.023 ms
 Execution Time: 106.375 ms

Using GIN:

CREATE INDEX ix_gin_tickers ON article USING GIN (tickers)

There we see "Index scan"

QUERY PLAN (after index)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on public.article a  (cost=433.53..7343.29 rows=8516 width=126) (actual time=22.555..47.508 rows=343451.00 loops=1)
   Output: article_id, title, article_txt, tickers
   Recheck Cond: ('{AAPL,IBM,DELL,UNP}'::text[] && a.tickers)
   Heap Blocks: exact=6458
   Buffers: shared hit=6538
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on ix_gin_tickers  (cost=0.00..431.40 rows=8516 width=0) (actual time=21.933..21.934 rows=343451.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (a.tickers && '{AAPL,IBM,DELL,UNP}'::text[])
         Index Searches: 1
         Buffers: shared hit=80
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=23
 Planning Time: 0.143 ms
 Execution Time: 58.053 ms

Example fiddle

I think that if the query results in a significantly smaller number of rows — a more selective query than the one in my example (80 %) — the difference in performance will be more noticeable.

Q: How do I copy Data Validation List from one cell to another using Excel VBA? A:

As this answer by MGonet mentions, the issue here is that the Input for Formula1 has to be an International-style formula; while the Output is in a Local-style formula.

This means that, for example, if your Local language uses Commas for decimals and semi-colons for functions, then they will not match:

#International
1 ÷ 2 = 0.5
MAX(0, 5) = 5

#Local (Spanish)
1 ÷ 2 = 0,5
MAX(0; 5) = 5
MAX(0,5) = 0,5

While Excel does have the Application.ConvertFormula method, that is for converting between A1-notation and R1C1-notation — not for converting regions.

The function/module listed below will convert between regions. However, since it relies somewhat on the behaviour of the LAMBDA function, it will only work in Excel 2024 or later (including an up-to-date version of Excel 365)

(It uses Names rather than editing a Range or Cell, because that should cause fewer potential issues with the workbook: no need to find a blank cell to work with, or to add temporary Worksheets/Workbooks)

Option Private Module
Option Explicit

Public Enum xlRegionStyle
    xlLocal = 1
    xlInternational = -4150
End Enum

Public Function ConvertFormulaRegion(Formula As Variant, FromRegionStyle As xlRegionStyle, ToRegionStyle As xlRegionStyle) As Variant
    'If no conversion is necessary, skip it all
    If ToRegionStyle = FromRegionStyle Then
        ConvertFormulaRegion = Formula
        Exit Function
    End If
    
    'Generate a random name; hopefully this won't clash with any that already exist
    Dim tempName As String: tempName = "_" & Right("0000" & Hex(Int(Rnd() * 65536)), 4) & "_" & Right("0000" & Hex(Int(Rnd() * 65536)), 4) & "_" & Right("0000" & Hex(Int(Rnd() * 65536)), 4) & "_" & Right("0000" & Hex(Int(Rnd() * 65536)), 4)
    
    On Error GoTo HadErr
    
    Dim RawFormula As String, HasEquals As Boolean, WorkingFormula As String
    
    'Do we have a full Formula, or just a subset?
    RawFormula = CStr(Formula)
    HasEquals = False
    If Left(RawFormula, 1) = "=" Then
        'If a full Formula, remove the "=", and remember that we need to restore it later
        HasEquals = True
        RawFormula = Mid(RawFormula, 2)
    End If
    
    If FromRegionStyle = xlLocal Then
        ThisWorkbook.Names.Add Name:=tempName, RefersTo:="=LAMBDA(1)"
        
        'Work out what the Local version of LAMBDA is
        WorkingFormula = ThisWorkbook.Names(tempName).RefersToLocal
        ThisWorkbook.Names(tempName).Delete
        'Place the Fomula inside the LAMBDA
        ThisWorkbook.Names.Add Name:=tempName, RefersToLocal:=Replace(WorkingFormula, "(1)", "(" & RawFormula & ")")
        'Get the International version
        WorkingFormula = ThisWorkbook.Names(tempName).RefersTo
    Else
        'Set the International version
        ThisWorkbook.Names.Add Name:=tempName, RefersTo:="=LAMBDA(" & RawFormula & ")"
        'Get the Local version
        WorkingFormula = ThisWorkbook.Names(tempName).RefersToLocal
    End If
    ThisWorkbook.Names(tempName).Delete
    
    'Strip the LAMBDA
    WorkingFormula = Mid(WorkingFormula, InStr(WorkingFormula, "(") + 1)
    WorkingFormula = Left(WorkingFormula, Len(WorkingFormula) - 1)
    
    'Restore the initial "=" if required, and return the result
    ConvertFormulaRegion = IIf(HasEquals, "=", "") & WorkingFormula
    Exit Function
HadErr:
    'Something has gone wrong
    On Error Resume Next
    'Try to tidy up
    ThisWorkbook.Names(tempName).Delete
    On Error GoTo -1 'Clear errors
    On Error GoTo 0
    ConvertFormulaRegion = CVErr(xlErrNA) 'Return an error
End Function

This can then be fed back into the Validation code to convert your list/formula, like so:

Formula1:=ConvertFormulaRegion(cellToCopy.Validation.Formula1, xlLocal, xlInternational)

Q: Initialize multiple static data members via a function A:

Everything boils down to a simple fact: standard C++ does not have static constructors.

The idea given to you in this Gemini answer was a known trick of using a single static initialization function and calling it to perform a fake “initialization” of a dummy private static member (token), as shown in your code sample.

You can only initialize a static member with a static function, but a member cannot have the type void. So the idea is using a fake assignment target of some type. It can be anything, including bool.

The fake initialization itself does not mean anything. This is just a placeholder. The real desired effect of your function init is two assignments, and not return. That return is just required syntactically.

This solution is not perfect because it still holds a dead piece of memory allocated for token in your process's static memory space.

Can you find a better solution? It depends on your criteria. It soulds weird that you find the solution you show hard to understand. Just the opposite: it is more readable, maintainable and easy to understand.

The other solution would be a classical out of class initialization: calling a public static initialization function. In contrast to the solution you've shown, it won't waste memory spend on token. But this classical solution would require you using non-public initialization function and remembering the place where you should call it in the entire application runtime (to be called exactly once, strictly before any other code uses your class's data, and so on). This is less maitainable.

Both solutions can be used. You decide.

Q: Bubble tree in D3.js A:

You can use the pack layout. Basically, you can bind any data you want to the shapes in the graph and custom parameters for them to position well respect to each other.

Another alternative would be the force layout.

Q: Retry failed after 4 tries. Retry settings can be adjusted in ClientOptions.Retry. (The SSL connection could not be established) accessing keyvault A:

My understanding is that the Key Vault was not available for some reason or, since the error mentions an SSL connection, there was an error specifically with the SSL certificate. For example, we experienced a similar error when our Kubernetes cluster was modified (upgraded). The error could also have to do with Azure not being available or maybe even not having network connectivity for a while.

Q: SQL Error: ORA-02315: incorrect number of arguments for default constructor A:

In my case, the error was due to the type object was outdated - one column was missing in the type structure in the database I'm working on (i.e. a copy from a development enviroment).

Once I added the missing column in the type and re-create it, the problem was solved.

Q: HTTP 400 Bad Request - Invalid Header with Retrofit on Android A:

Not sure what the server expects as a header parameter, but you can pass any header value on the client interface

@PUT("/<path>")
Response updateThing(@Header("headerName") String headerName, @Body Dto dto);
